subject: 🏭 Uneven factory comeback
body_html:
Plus: French spillovers | Thursday, October 22, 2026
 
View in browser
 
 
Axios Macro
By Neil Irwin and Courtenay Brown · Oct 22, 2026

U.S. manufacturers are emerging from a yearslong slump. But look under the hood, and the sector's rebound isn't being evenly felt across America's factories.

  • What's driving the industrial surge? We have answers below.
  • Plus, how the latest French bond drama spills over to U.S. markets.

Situational awareness: New applications for unemployment benefits fell by 6,000, to 194,000 last week. That makes six consecutive weeks with claims at or below 200,000, as employers remain reluctant to shed workers.

Today's newsletter, edited by Jeffrey Cane and copy edited by Katie Lewis, is 881 words, a 3.5-minute read.
 
 
1 big thing: Two-speed factory recovery
 

Illustration: Aïda Amer/Axios
 

American manufacturing is showing signs of revival. But the recovery is being powered by industries at the forefront of the AI and energy boom while the traditional factory sector gets left behind.

Why it matters: The White House is touting a revival in American manufacturing as evidence that its economic agenda is working.

  • But a lopsided recovery raises questions about how much of the sector stands to benefit — especially as higher borrowing costs threaten to weigh on factories once again.

Zoom in: Factory output rose 0.3% in September despite a 3% drop in auto production — the latest evidence that the long-struggling sector is gaining momentum.

  • The Institute for Supply Management's manufacturing index showed a ninth straight month of expansion, with new orders growing at a faster pace and backlogs of unfinished work mounting.

Yes, but: The pickup in the headline manufacturing sector is not translating into hiring across the board.

  • Last month, five of the six largest manufacturing industries reported rising new orders, but only two — computers and electronics, and transportation equipment — reported increased employment, ISM said.

The striking split is evident in the hard employment data, according to an analysis by Gad Levanon, chief economist at the Burning Glass Institute.

  • U.S. manufacturers added a net 40,000 jobs over the 12 months ending in September. But the gains came entirely from advanced manufacturing — even though the subset accounts for just 38% of factory employment, Levanon wrote.
  • Those industries — including chemicals, machinery, computers and electronics, and transportation equipment — added 56,000 jobs over that period. Every other manufacturing industry combined lost 16,000 jobs, offsetting part of those gains.
  • Employment outside advanced manufacturing is barely above its 2016 level, reflecting years of stagnation across much of the factory sector.

What they're saying: "So the manufacturing recovery is real, but it is narrow," Levanon wrote.

  • The recovery is "happening in the industries that make the equipment for the AI and energy buildout and in the ones most affected by reshoring. The rest of the factory sector is not hiring, and I don't expect that to change soon," he added.

What to watch: The Fed's latest tightening cycle could widen the divide between American manufacturers before threatening the recovery itself, James Knightley, chief international economist at ING, tells Axios.

  • Traditional, labor-intensive producers are already struggling with high costs and foreign competition. Advanced manufacturers, meanwhile, are benefiting from an AI and energy investment boom that could help sustain growth despite higher borrowing costs.
  • If borrowing costs keep climbing and investors begin questioning tech valuations, even the advanced industries driving the recovery could come under pressure.
  • "This need for external financing creates a vulnerability that could translate into a slowdown in the sector," Knightley says.

2. Les effets de débordement
 
Data: FactSet; Chart: Neil Irwin/Axios

The unrelenting sell-off in French bonds has continued today. The latest move shows how that nation's precarious fiscal and political situation could spill over elsewhere — including offering relief for U.S. borrowing costs.

The big picture: U.S. Treasury yields have fallen in the last couple of weeks, while French borrowing costs have surged. Borrowing costs are also down in other traditional safe-haven nations.

  • This may partly reflect investors seeking alternatives to French bonds, alongside a broader safe-haven effect as there have been new wobbles in AI-related debt markets.

Driving the news: The effect is particularly pronounced in today's trading. As of 11:30am ET, 10-year French government bond yields were up another 0.08 percentage point, to 5.07%, a new 24-year high.

  • Yields on the 10-year U.S. Treasury, meanwhile, were down 0.12 point, to 5.02%, the lowest since Sept. 22. That rate reached 5.31%, a multidecade high, just over two weeks ago on Oct. 5.
  • Sovereign bond yields are also down sharply today for Germany, Canada and Switzerland.

State of play: The overall action in financial markets today fits a classic "risk-off" pattern, with global stocks falling and money flowing into bonds of most countries other than France.

  • In effect, French fiscal troubles have made a significant pool of global safe assets look significantly less safe — and U.S. debt comparatively attractive.

What they're saying: "Treasuries are benefiting from France's deteriorating debt dynamics and bond market turmoil," Michael Pedroni, CEO of Highland Global Advisors and a former Treasury official, tells Axios.

  • "While the U.S. debt outlook is troubling, market participants continue to treat Treasuries as a safe haven," he adds. "Safety is relative."
  • "In contrast, French bonds appear to carry substantial credit risk, given the country's anemic growth, mounting debt fueled by an overly generous pension system, social unrest and signals that the European Central Bank may wait for conditions to worsen before intervening."

The bottom line: The French term for spillover effects is "effets de débordement," online translators tell us. It's a phrase with which everyone may wish to familiarize themselves.
